about: Planetary Maps: the places marked on the Moon and Mars maps. Written by hand; positions checked Nov 17, 2026 against NASA Trek's IAU feature names (craters, mountains, valleys, plains) and Trek's landing-site areas, and landing points against NASA's mission pages (docs/DATA-SOURCES.md, Planetary Maps). Latitude north positive, longitude east positive (-180 to 180). group: land (landing site), crater, volc (volcano or mountain), valley (valley, canyon or plain).

mars.name: Jezero Crater
facts: Perseverance and the Ingenuity helicopter, February 18, 2021
25 cm a pixel over the crater floor and delta (HiRISE), 6 m around it
mars.text: A crater that held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago. A river flowed in through a gap in the western rim and left a fan of mud and sand, the delta: the reason Perseverance was sent here. Rocks from the delta, which could hold signs of ancient life, are sealed in sample tubes. Ingenuity, the first helicopter to fly on another world, made 72 flights here.

picture.alt: Jezero crater and the land around it in colour, seen from above by ESA's Mars Express: highlands, dark dunes of volcanic ash and the crater with its delta
picture.caption: Jezero and its surroundings, from ESA's Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera.

mars.name: Gale Crater
mars.text: A huge crater with a mountain in the middle, Aeolis Mons ("Mount Sharp"), built of layers laid down in lakes and later by wind. Curiosity is climbing it layer by layer, reading the history of Mars' climate like the pages of a book.

picture.alt: Gale crater seen from above by ESA's Mars Express, coloured by height: the low crater floor in blue and the central mountain in red and white
picture.caption: Gale coloured by height (blue low, white high), from ESA's Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera, 100 m a pixel.

mars.name: Aeolis Mons
facts: About 5 km above the crater floor
mars.text: The layered mountain in the middle of Gale Crater. Its lowest layers formed in water; higher up the rocks change, recording how Mars dried out. Curiosity has been climbing its lower slopes since 2014.

mars.name: Olympus Mons
facts: About 600 km across and 22 km high
mars.text: The tallest volcano in the solar system, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level. Its slopes are so gentle and it is so wide that someone standing on the top would not see that they were on a mountain.

mars.name: Ascraeus Mons
facts: The northern of the three Tharsis volcanoes
mars.text: One of three giant volcanoes standing in a line on the Tharsis bulge, a raised region of lava the size of a continent.

mars.name: Pavonis Mons
facts: The middle of the three Tharsis volcanoes, on the equator
mars.text: The middle volcano of the Tharsis line. Like its neighbours it is a shield volcano: built by runny lava flowing out over a very long time, like the volcanoes of Hawaii but much bigger.

mars.name: Arsia Mons
facts: The southern of the three Tharsis volcanoes
mars.text: The southern volcano of the Tharsis line, with a summit crater about 110 km across. A long, thin cloud often forms over it in the early morning.

mars.name: Elysium Mons
facts: The Elysium volcanic region, on the other side of Mars from Tharsis
mars.text: The largest volcano of Mars' second volcanic region. NASA's InSight lander measured marsquakes on the plains to its south.

mars.name: Valles Marineris
facts: More than 4,000 km long and up to about 7 km deep
mars.text: A system of canyons as long as the United States is wide. It formed as the crust cracked and pulled apart beside the Tharsis volcanoes, then was widened by landslides. It is named after Mariner 9, the orbiter that found it in 1971.

mars.name: Hellas Planitia
facts: About 2,300 km across and 7 km deep
mars.text: One of the largest impact craters in the solar system, made by a huge collision about 4 billion years ago. Its floor is the lowest ground on Mars, where the air is thickest.

mars.name: Argyre Planitia
mars.text: A large impact basin in the southern highlands, ringed by mountains thrown up by the collision that made it.

mars.name: Ares Vallis
facts: Mars Pathfinder landed at its mouth in 1997
mars.text: A channel cut by enormous floods that once poured north across the plains. Pathfinder was sent to its mouth to find rocks washed down from the highlands.

mars.name: Viking 1
mars.text: The first lander to work on Mars for a long time, and NASA's first on another planet. It sent back the first pictures from the surface and tested the soil for signs of life.

mars.name: Viking 2
mars.text: Viking 1's twin, on the northern plains. It photographed frost on the ground in the Martian winter.

mars.name: Mars Pathfinder
facts: Sojourner, the first rover on Mars
mars.text: Landed by bouncing on airbags. Its small rover, Sojourner, drove about 100 m in total, studying the rocks around the lander.

mars.name: Spirit
mars.text: Planned for 90 days, Spirit worked for six years. In the Columbia Hills it found rocks altered by hot water, and silica left by ancient hot springs.

mars.name: Opportunity
mars.text: Planned for 90 days, it lasted more than 14 years, until a planet-wide dust storm. Small round grains it found, nicknamed "blueberries", formed in water soaking through the rock.

mars.name: Phoenix
mars.text: Dug into the ground near the north polar cap and found water ice just under the soil.

mars.name: InSight
mars.text: Listened to the inside of Mars. Its seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes, which showed how thick the crust is and how big the core is.

mars.name: Zhurong (CNSA)
mars.text: China's first Mars rover. It drove about 1.9 km before going to sleep for the winter in May 2022, and did not wake again.

mars.name: Gusev Crater
mars.text: Chosen for Spirit because a long valley, Ma'adim Vallis, runs into it, so it may once have held a lake. Spirit found volcanic rock on its floor and signs of hot water in the Columbia Hills.

mars.name: Endeavour Crater
mars.text: Opportunity drove for three years to reach it and then explored its rim for seven more, finding veins of gypsum left by water flowing through cracks.

mars.name: Korolev Crater
mars.text: Filled with a mound of water ice about 1.8 km thick that stays all year. Air over the ice is cold, so it acts as a trap that keeps the ice from turning to vapour.

mars.name: Planum Boreum
facts: About 1,000 km across and up to 3 km thick
mars.text: A dome of water ice in thin layers, laid down over millions of years as Mars' climate changed. Spiral troughs cut into it by wind make it look like a swirl from above.

mars.name: Planum Australe
facts: Layers of water ice and dust, topped with frozen carbon dioxide
mars.text: The south polar ice. Each winter carbon dioxide from the air freezes onto it, and in spring it turns back into gas, changing the air pressure all over Mars by about a quarter.

mars.name: Utopia Planitia
mars.text: The largest known impact basin on Mars, filled in to make a vast plain. Radar from orbit found a layer of buried ice beneath part of it holding about as much water as Lake Superior.

moon.name: Apollo 11
facts: About 0.5 m a pixel (LRO Narrow Angle Camera)
moon.text: The first landing by people. Zoom in to see the descent stage of the lunar module Eagle, photographed by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, still standing where it landed.

moon.name: Apollo 12
moon.text: A pinpoint landing within walking distance of Surveyor 3, a robot lander that had arrived two and a half years earlier. The crew brought parts of it back to Earth.

moon.name: Apollo 14
moon.text: Explored rocks thrown out by the impact that made the Imbrium basin. Alan Shepard hit two golf balls here.

moon.name: Apollo 15
moon.text: The first mission with the Lunar Roving Vehicle, at the foot of the Apennine mountains beside a winding lava channel. The crew found the "Genesis Rock", a piece of the Moon's ancient crust.

moon.name: Apollo 16
moon.text: The only Apollo landing in the bright highlands. Geologists expected volcanic rock; the crew found mostly rock broken and welded together by impacts.

moon.name: Apollo 17
moon.text: The last time people walked on the Moon so far. Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, found orange soil made of tiny glass beads from an ancient volcanic eruption.

moon.name: Chang'e 4 (CNSA)
moon.text: The first landing on the far side of the Moon, which never faces the Earth. Its rover, Yutu-2, explored the floor of Von Kármán crater, inside the huge South Pole–Aitken basin.

moon.name: Chang'e 5 (CNSA)
moon.text: The first samples brought back from the Moon since 1976. They come from some of its youngest lava, about 2 billion years old.

moon.name: Chang'e 6 (CNSA)
moon.text: The first samples ever brought back from the far side of the Moon.

moon.name: Chandrayaan-3 (ISRO)
moon.text: India's lander Vikram and its rover Pragyan, the first to land this close to the Moon's south pole, where ice may lie in craters that sunlight never reaches.

moon.name: Tycho
facts: About 100 million years: young for the Moon
moon.text: A young, sharp crater whose bright rays of thrown-out rock stretch across much of the near side. At full Moon it is easy to see from Earth with binoculars.

moon.name: Copernicus
moon.text: A classic crater with terraced walls and mountains in the middle, pushed up by the rebound of the ground after the impact.

moon.name: Shackleton
moon.text: Sits almost exactly on the south pole. Its rim gets sunlight most of the time, but its floor never does, so it is one of the coldest places known and may hold ice. The flat map stretches it sideways near the pole.

moon.name: Mare Tranquillitatis
facts: A plain of dark, solidified lava
moon.text: The dark patches seen on the Moon from Earth are "seas" (maria): huge plains of lava that filled old impact basins more than 3 billion years ago. Apollo 11 landed at this one's south-western edge.

moon.name: Cabeus
moon.text: NASA crashed the spent rocket stage of its LCROSS mission into a permanently dark part of this crater on October 9, 2009, and measured the plume that rose out of it: it held water ice.

moon.name: Haworth
moon.text: Its floor lies in permanent shadow and is one of the places where ice may be trapped. The region around it is on NASA's list of possible landing regions for the first crewed landing near the south pole.

moon.name: Faustini
moon.text: Sunlight never reaches its floor. LRO's instruments map such permanently shadowed craters by the faint light reflected from nearby peaks and by their own warmth.

moon.name: Amundsen
moon.text: A large crater with central peaks, named after Roald Amundsen, who led the first expedition to reach the Earth's South Pole.

moon.name: Mons Mouton
facts: 2022, after Melba Roy Mouton, a NASA mathematician
moon.text: A broad, flat-topped mountain several kilometres high near the south pole. It was named when NASA studied landing regions for its crewed missions; Intuitive Machines' lander Athena came down near it in March 2025.

moon.name: Malapert
facts: Beside the Malapert massif, a mountain that can often see the Earth
moon.text: The mountains around Malapert are high enough to stay in sunlight much of the time and to keep the Earth above the horizon, which makes them attractive for future landings.

moon.name: Odysseus (Intuitive Machines)
moon.text: The first landing on the Moon by a private company, and the first American landing since Apollo 17. It tipped onto its side as it landed but kept working for about a week.

moon.name: Peary
moon.text: Near the Moon's north pole. Parts of its rim are lit by the Sun for most of the lunar year, so it has been studied as a place for solar power.

moon.name: Hermite
moon.text: Parts of its floor are among the coldest places ever measured in the solar system, colder than the surface of Pluto, because sunlight never reaches them.

moon.name: Chang'e 3 (CNSA)
moon.text: The first soft landing on the Moon since 1976, and China's first. Its rover Yutu used ground-penetrating radar to look at the layers of lava beneath it.

moon.name: Luna 9 (Soviet Union)
moon.text: The first spacecraft to land softly on the Moon and send pictures from the surface. It showed that the ground was firm enough to stand on.

moon.name: Lunokhod 1 (Soviet Union)
moon.text: The first remote-controlled rover on another world, driven by a team on Earth for ten months. A reflector on it still bounces laser pulses back from Earth.
